grammar.title: Present perfect with for and since; How long…?
grammar.summary: Use the present perfect with 'for' and 'since' for situations that started in the past and are still true now. 'For' + a period of time (for three years); 'since' + the starting point (since 2021). Ask with 'How long have you…?'
grammar.summaryMn: Өнгөрсөнд эхэлсэн, одоо ч үргэлжилж байгаа байдлын тухай ярихад present perfect-ийг 'for', 'since'-тэй хэрэглэнэ. 'For' + хугацааны урт (for three years — гурван жил), 'since' + эхэлсэн цэг (since 2021 — 2021 оноос хойш). 'How long have you…?' гэж асууна.
structure: have/has + past participle + for + a period of time → I've worked here for five years.
have/has + past participle + since + a starting point → She's been a manager since March.
Question: How long + have/has + subject + past participle? → How long have you known Bat?
for: two weeks, six months, ten years, ages, a long time · since: Monday, 2019, last summer, I was a child, I left school
Finished situations use the past simple, even with for → I worked in a bank for two years (I don't work there now).

usage.use: A situation that started in the past and continues now
usage.example: I've lived in Ulaanbaatar for ten years.
usage.useMn: Өнгөрсөнд эхэлж, одоо ч үргэлжилж буй байдал

usage.example: He's been unemployed for six months.
We've known each other since university.

usage.use: Asking about the length of time: How long…?
usage.example: How long have you had this job?
usage.useMn: Хэр удаж байгааг асуух: How long…?

usage.use: Finished situations use the past simple, even with 'for'
usage.example: My father worked as a driver for thirty years. He retired in 2020.
usage.useMn: Дууссан байдалд 'for'-той байсан ч past simple хэрэглэнэ

examples.en: I've worked at this company since March, so I've been here for about six months.
How long have you been a teacher? — For twelve years.
examples.note: The short answer can be just 'For…' or 'Since…'.

examples.en: She hasn't seen her family since the New Year holiday.
examples.note: Negative sentences work in the same way.

examples.en: My grandmother worked in a factory for twenty years.
examples.note: She doesn't work there now → past simple.

pairs.a: I've lived here for five years.
pairs.why: The present perfect + for/since says how long, from the past until now. The present simple only describes now.
pairs.whyMn: Present perfect + for/since нь өнгөрсөнөөс одоог хүртэл хэр удсаныг хэлнэ. Present simple зөвхөн одоогийн байдлыг хэлнэ.

pairs.a: I've worked there for two years.
pairs.b: I worked there for two years.
pairs.why: The first person still works there. The second person doesn't work there any more.
pairs.whyMn: Эхнийх нь одоо ч тэнд ажиллаж байгаа. Хоёр дахь нь одоо тэнд ажиллахаа больсон.

mistakes.why: For a situation from the past until now, use the present perfect, not the present simple.
mistakes.whyMn: Өнгөрсөнөөс одоог хүртэлх байдалд present simple биш present perfect хэрэглэнэ.

mistakes.wrong: I've known him since five years.

mistakes.why: 'Five years' is a period of time, so use 'for'.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Five years' бол хугацааны урт тул 'for' хэрэглэнэ.

mistakes.right: How long have you worked here?
mistakes.why: 'How long' + from the past until now → present perfect.
mistakes.whyMn: Өнгөрсөнөөс одоог хүртэлх хугацааг асуухад present perfect хэрэглэнэ.

mistakes.right: I've been married for ten years.
mistakes.why: Use have/has + been, not am/is/are, with 'for' and 'since'.

grammar.title: Present perfect with just, already and yet
grammar.summary: Use 'just' for something that happened a very short time ago, 'already' for something that happened before now (often sooner than expected), and 'yet' in questions and negatives for something we expect to happen. In British English all three usually go with the present perfect.
grammar.summaryMn: 'Just' — дөнгөж сая болсон үйл, 'already' — аль хэдийн (ихэвчлэн хүлээснээс эрт) болсон үйл, 'yet' — асуулт болон үгүйсгэлд хэрэглэгдэх, болох ёстой ч хараахан болоогүй үйл. Британи англи хэлэнд гурвуулаа ихэвчлэн present perfect-тэй хэрэглэгдэнэ.
structure: just: have/has + just + past participle → I've just sent the email.
already: have/has + already + past participle → She's already finished the report.
yet (negative): haven't/hasn't + past participle + … + yet → I haven't replied yet.
yet (question): Have/Has + subject + past participle + … + yet? → Have you called the client yet?
Word order: just and already go between have and the past participle; yet goes at the end.

usage.use: just = a very short time ago
already = before now, maybe earlier than expected
usage.example: Don't worry, I've already booked the meeting room.

usage.use: not … yet = it hasn't happened, but we expect it to happen
usage.example: We haven't received the contract yet.
usage.useMn: not … yet — хараахан болоогүй (гэхдээ болно гэж хүлээж байгаа)

usage.use: Questions with yet = asking if something expected has happened
usage.example: Have you had any feedback yet?
usage.useMn: yet-тэй асуулт — хүлээж буй зүйл болсон эсэхийг асуух

examples.en: I've just finished the presentation. Shall I send it to you now?
Have you signed the contract yet? — Yes, I've already signed it and sent it back.
examples.note: yet in the question, already in the answer.

examples.en: The new manager hasn't started yet. She starts on Monday.
examples.note: We expect it to happen soon.

examples.en: It's only ten o'clock and I've already had three meetings!
I just sent it. / Did you eat yet?
examples.note: American English often uses the past simple with just, already and yet. You will hear it, but this course uses the British form.

contrast.with: Past simple with a finished time

pairs.b: I saw the email ten minutes ago.
pairs.why: 'Just' + present perfect gives no exact time. With an exact finished time ('ten minutes ago'), use the past simple.
pairs.whyMn: 'Just' + present perfect-д тодорхой цаг хэлдэггүй. Дууссан тодорхой цагтай ('ten minutes ago') бол past simple хэрэглэнэ.

pairs.a: Have you finished the report yet?
pairs.b: Did you finish the report yesterday?
pairs.why: Up to now (no finished time) vs a finished time (yesterday).
pairs.whyMn: Одоог хүртэл (дууссан цаггүй) ба дууссан тодорхой цаг (yesterday).

mistakes.wrong: I have finished already the report.
mistakes.right: I've already finished the report. / I've finished the report already.
mistakes.why: 'Already' goes between have and the past participle, or at the very end — not between the verb and its object.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Already' нь have ба V3-ын хооронд, эсвэл өгүүлбэрийн төгсгөлд байрлана; үйл үг ба тусагдахууны хооронд орохгүй.

mistakes.right: I've already finished. / I haven't finished yet.
mistakes.why: 'Yet' is for questions and negatives. In positive sentences use 'already'.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Yet'-ийг асуулт, үгүйсгэлд хэрэглэнэ. Эерэг өгүүлбэрт 'already' хэрэглэнэ.

mistakes.right: I sent it yesterday. / I've just sent it.
mistakes.why: Don't use the present perfect with a finished time like 'yesterday'.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Yesterday' шиг дууссан цагтай present perfect хэрэглэхгүй.

mistakes.why: After has/have, use the past participle (gone), not the past simple (went).
mistakes.whyMn: has/have-ийн дараа V3 (gone) хэрэглэнэ, V2 (went) биш.

guided.prompt: Can you call back later? Tsetseg has ___ left the office.
guided.explanation: She left a very short time ago → just.

guided.prompt: I haven't read the new contract ___.

options: Have you replied to the client yet?
Have you replied yet to the client already?

Between have and the past participle
At the end of the sentence
At the start of the sentence

free.explanation: Question about something expected → yet at the end.

answers: I have already sent the invoice.

free.explanation: 'Already' goes before the past participle or at the end.

The new designer has not arrived yet.

free.explanation: Expected but not happened → hasn't + past participle + yet.

pronunciation.title: Word stress in job words: -tion, -ity, -ence, -ment
pronunciation.explanation: Long job words are hard to understand if the stress is in the wrong place. Some endings help you. Words ending in -tion are stressed on the syllable just before the ending (qualifiCAtion, proMOtion). Words ending in -ity are stressed on the syllable just before -ity (responsiBILity, opporTUnity). Endings like -ment and -er don't change the stress of the base word (aCHIEVE → aCHIEVEment, emPLOY → emPLOYer). The unstressed syllables are short and weak, often with /ə/.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Урт үгийн өргөлт буруу байвал ойлгоход хэцүү. Зарим дагавар тусална: -tion-оор төгссөн үгийн өргөлт дагаврын яг өмнөх үе дээр (qualifiCAtion, proMOtion). -ity-гаар төгссөн үгийн өргөлт -ity-ийн яг өмнөх үе дээр (responsiBILity, opporTUnity). -ment, -er дагавар үндсэн үгийн өргөлтийг өөрчилдөггүй (aCHIEVE → aCHIEVEment). Өргөлтгүй үеүд богино, сул, ихэвчлэн /ə/ болно.

items.tip: -tion: stress the syllable just before it.
-ity: stress the syllable just before it.
-ment doesn't change the stress: aCHIEVE → aCHIEVEment.

shadowing.text: I've got the right qualifications and five years of experience.
shadowing.stress: I've got the RIGHT qualifiCAtions and FIVE YEARS of exPErience.
shadowing.tip: Say the weak first syllables quickly: /kwɒl/ and /ɪk/.

shadowing.text: This job is a great opportunity to take on more responsibility.
shadowing.stress: This JOB is a GREAT opporTUnity to take ON MORE responsiBILity.
shadowing.tip: Both long words have the stress just before -ity.

shadowing.text: Getting a promotion was my biggest achievement last year.
shadowing.stress: GETting a proMOtion was my BIGgest aCHIEVEment last YEAR.
shadowing.tip: Promotion: three syllables, stress in the middle.

lessons.title: A new career at thirty-six
objectives: Use 11 words and collocations about jobs and careers
Understand the main idea and details of a magazine article about changing careers
Talk about career plans with collocations like 'gain experience' and 'get a promotion'

warmup.intro: What did you want to be when you were a child? Is your job (or your plan) the same now?

questions.prompt: The money you get every month for your job is your…
The article in this lesson is called 'A New Career at Thirty-Six'. What do you think happens?
options: Someone leaves one kind of work and starts a very different one.
Someone retires from work at thirty-six.
Someone gets their very first job at thirty-six.

vocabulary.definition: the series of jobs you do in your working life, usually in one area
examples: She has had a long career in banking.
I'm thinking about a career change.
vocabulary.mistake: A career is your whole working life, not one job: 'I'm looking for a job', not 'I'm looking for a career' when you mean one position. Pronounce it ka-REER, not like 'carrier'.

vocabulary.definition: an official certificate or exam result that shows you have the knowledge or skills for a job
examples: She got her first qualification in web design after a year of study.
What qualifications do you need to become a pilot?
vocabulary.mistake: Don't confuse 'qualification' (a certificate or degree) with 'quality' (how good something is).

vocabulary.definition: the knowledge and skills you get from doing a job for some time
examples: She has ten years of experience in marketing.
An internship is a good way to gain experience.
vocabulary.mistake: In this meaning it's uncountable: 'three years of experience', not 'three years experiences'.
vocabulary.note: Countable 'an experience' is something that happened to you: 'a memorable experience'.

vocabulary.definition: to ask formally, usually in writing, for a job or a place at a university
examples: I've applied for three jobs this month.
Many people never apply for their dream job.
vocabulary.mistake: You apply FOR a job and TO a company: 'I applied for the manager position', not 'I applied to the manager position'.

vocabulary.definition: a job in a company or organisation (formal)
examples: She applied for a junior position at a tech company.
We are looking for someone to fill the position of sales manager.
vocabulary.note: More formal than 'job'. Common in job adverts and formal emails.

vocabulary.definition: the fixed amount of money you get for your job, usually every month
examples: Her new salary was almost half of her old one.
The job offers a good salary and flexible hours.
vocabulary.mistake: We 'earn' or 'get' a salary, not 'take' a salary. A 'wage' is usually paid per hour or per week.

vocabulary.definition: a person who is paid to work for a company or another person
examples: The company has over two hundred employees.
As an employee of a large bank, she had a safe job.
vocabulary.mistake: An employee works for someone; an employer (the company or boss) pays them. The stress is at the end: em-ploy-EE.

vocabulary.definition: a chance to do something good or useful
examples: This job is a great opportunity to learn new skills.
Look for opportunities to practise your English at work.
vocabulary.mistake: Mongolian 'боломж' can be 'opportunity' or 'possibility'. For a good chance, say 'an opportunity to work abroad', not 'a possibility to work abroad'.

vocabulary.definition: a move to a higher and more important job in the same company
examples: Eighteen months later, she got a promotion.
He's hoping for a promotion this year.
vocabulary.note: Verb: be promoted — 'She was promoted to manager.'

vocabulary.definition: something good that you have done successfully, usually with a lot of effort
examples: Getting the qualification was a big achievement for her.
What is your greatest achievement so far?
vocabulary.mistake: Don't say 'I achieved a success'. Say 'It was a great achievement' or 'I achieved my goal'.

vocabulary.definition: wanting very much to be successful
examples: Ambitious people often feel stuck in safe jobs.
She's very ambitious — she wants to be a director by forty.
vocabulary.note: Usually positive in English, but 'too ambitious' about a plan means 'not realistic'.

reading.title: A New Career at Thirty-Six
text: For twelve years, Enkhjargal Batbold had a safe job and a good salary. She was an employee of one of the biggest banks in Ulaanbaatar, where she worked as an accountant, and her parents were very proud of her. 'Everyone thought I had the perfect career,' she says. 'But every Sunday evening I felt sick when I thought about Monday.'

At thirty-five, she started an online course in web design. She studied late at night and at weekends, and a year later she got her first qualification. Then she did something that surprised everyone: she left the bank and applied for a junior position at a small tech company. She got the job, but her new salary was almost half of her old one.

'The first months were really hard,' she remembers. 'The other designers were ten years younger than me, and they knew much more than I did. But I had one big advantage: experience. I understood how companies work, how to talk to clients and how to organise my time.' Her manager noticed. Eighteen months later, Enkhjargal got a promotion, and she has led a small team of designers since then.

Career coaches say her story is not unusual. Many people in their thirties and forties dream of a new career, but they never apply for a different job because they are afraid of failing. 'Ambitious people often feel stuck in safe jobs,' explains career coach Oyun Dorj. 'My advice is to start small. Take a course, talk to people who do the job you want, and look for opportunities to try it before you leave your old job.'
Does Enkhjargal have any regrets? 'Only one,' she laughs. 'I didn't do it sooner.' And her biggest achievement? It isn't the promotion, she says. 'It's that I enjoy Mondays now.'

at a low level in a company, often new
unable to change or move forward

vocabulary.definition: a person you work with
examples: I've known my colleague Tuvshin since we both started here.

vocabulary.mistake: Stress the first syllable: KOL-eeg. For people you study with, say 'classmate', not 'colleague'.

vocabulary.definition: one part of a large company or organisation
examples: She works in the sales department.
I've been in the IT department for two years.

vocabulary.definition: all the people who work for an organisation
examples: All staff must attend the meeting on Friday.
We have fifty members of staff.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Staff' is a group noun: 'fifty members of staff' or 'fifty staff', not 'fifty staffs'.

vocabulary.definition: for the whole of the normal working week
examples: I've had a full-time job since I graduated.

vocabulary.note: Write it with a hyphen, like 'part-time'.

vocabulary.definition: responsible for a group of people or an activity
examples: Who's in charge of the new project?

vocabulary.mistake: Say 'in charge of the team', not 'in charge for the team'.

vocabulary.definition: a duty to deal with something as part of your job; accepting that something is your fault

vocabulary.definition: an official written agreement, for example between a worker and a company
examples: I signed a one-year contract in January.

vocabulary.definition: without a paid job
examples: He's been unemployed for six months.
It's hard to stay positive when you're unemployed.

vocabulary.definition: to leave your job (informal)
examples: She quit her job at the bank last year.
Why did you quit your last job?
vocabulary.note: Irregular: quit – quit – quit. Informal; in formal writing use 'resign' or 'leave'.

vocabulary.definition: to stop working, usually because of your age
examples: My father retired three years ago.
My grandmother had to retire at fifty-five.
vocabulary.note: Noun: retirement. 'He's retired' = he doesn't work any more.

speaking.prompt: Describe your working life (or your studies). Say what you do now, how long you have done it, what your responsibilities are, and what you did before.
speaking.promptMn: Ажлын (эсвэл сурлагын) амьдралаа тайлбарла: одоо юу хийдэг, хэр удаж байгаа, ямар үүрэг хариуцлагатай, өмнө нь юу хийж байсан бэ.
points: Your job or studies now (present simple)
How long you have done it (for / since)
Your main responsibilities and your colleagues
What you did before (past simple)
phrases: I've been in the… department since…
speaking.sample: I'm an accountant. I've worked for a construction company in Ulaanbaatar for about five years. I started as a junior accountant, but since last year I've been in charge of salaries for the whole company, so I have much more responsibility now. I work full-time, from nine to six, and I share an office with three colleagues from the finance department. They're really friendly — I've known one of them since university. Before this job, I worked in a small shop for two years while I was studying. I enjoy my job, but one day I'd like to work abroad.

lessons.title: The job interview
objectives: Understand a job interview and the questions interviewers often ask
Talk about your strengths and weaknesses with natural phrases
Stress long job words correctly (qualifiCAtion, responsiBILity)
Answer interview questions in a role-play

warmup.intro: Have you ever had a job interview? How did you feel?

questions.prompt: Which question is very common in job interviews?
options: What are your strengths and weaknesses?

vocabulary.definition: a person who is trying to get a job, or who is taking an exam
examples: We've interviewed six candidates for the position.
She was the strongest candidate.

vocabulary.definition: a good quality or ability that makes someone effective
examples: What would you say are your main strengths?
Her biggest strength is her patience.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Strong' is the adjective; 'strength' is the noun. Say 'My main strength is…', not 'My main strong is…'.

vocabulary.definition: a quality or area where someone is not very good
examples: My biggest weakness is that I find it hard to say no.

vocabulary.note: In interviews, talk about a real weakness and say what you are doing to improve it.

lines.text: So, tell me a little about your current job. How long have you worked at Blue Sky Tours?

lines.speaker: Batbayar

vocabulary.definition: the amount of work a person has to do

phrases.meaning: a polite, friendly first line in an email
phrases.whenToUse: At the start of a work email to someone you know. 'I hope this email finds you well' is more formal and a bit old-fashioned.
phrases.example: Hi Anna, I hope you're well.

phrases.meaning: used to introduce short news about a piece of work
phrases.whenToUse: In the first line or subject of an email to colleagues or your manager. Friendly but professional — too casual for a first email to a new client.
phrases.example: Just a quick update on the training day.

phrases.meaning: I have added this file to the email
phrases.whenToUse: In formal emails, for example job applications. In everyday work emails, 'I've attached…' is also fine and sounds friendlier.
phrases.example: Please find attached my CV and a copy of my qualifications.

phrases.meaning: a polite way to ask for information or a decision
phrases.whenToUse: In emails and messages when you need an answer. Softer than 'Tell me…'.
phrases.example: Could you let me know if Thursday works for you?

phrases.whenToUse: When you reply a day or more after an email. In very formal emails: 'I apologise for the delay in replying.'
phrases.example: Sorry for the late reply — it's been a busy week.

phrases.meaning: standard ways to end a work email
phrases.whenToUse: To close work emails, with people you know or don't know. Don't use 'Speak soon' or 'Love' with people you don't know well.

writing.prompt: Your manager, Ms Davies, has asked for an update on an event you are organising (for example, a training day for new staff). Write an email. writing.sample:
Subject: Update on the staff training day

Dear Ms Davies,

I hope you're well. Just a quick update on the training day for new staff.

I've already booked the conference room and sent the invitations to all fifteen new employees. I've also just received the final programme from the trainer — I've attached it to this email. However, I haven't confirmed the lunch order yet, because the café hasn't replied.

My workload has been very heavy this week, so could we postpone our meeting from Wednesday to Friday morning? I'm available any time after 9:30.

Could you let me know if that works for you?

Kind regards,
Oyunaa

reading.title: Your First Job: Five Things Nobody Tells You
text: Starting your first full-time job is exciting, but it can also be confusing. University teaches you a lot, but it doesn't always prepare you for real office life. Here are five things I learned in my first year at work.
1. Nobody expects you to know everything. In your first few weeks, ask questions — lots of them. Your colleagues would much rather answer a simple question now than fix a big mistake later.

2. Write things down. You will get a lot of new information: names, passwords, how the printer works, who to ask about holidays. A small notebook will save you, and everyone around you, a lot of time.

3. Learn to say no politely. When you are new, it's tempting to say yes to every request because you want people to like you. But if you take on too much, you will start missing deadlines. It's better to say, 'I can do it, but not before Thursday.'

4. Ask for feedback. Don't wait for your yearly review to find out how you're doing. After a big task, ask your manager, 'Is there anything I could do better next time?' Most managers are happy that you asked.
5. Remember that your first job is not your whole career. If it isn't perfect, that's OK. Every job teaches you something, even if it only teaches you what you don't want to do.

speaking.sample: In my opinion, it depends on the person, but I think changing jobs every few years is usually a good idea, especially when you're young. When you move to a new company, you gain new experience, meet new colleagues and often get a higher salary. For example, my brother has changed jobs three times since he graduated, and each time he's learned something new. On the other hand, if you stay in one company for a long time, you can get a promotion and more responsibility. My mother has worked at the same school for twenty-five years, and now she's the head teacher. So both ways can work. Personally, I think the most important thing is to keep learning.
